title: Devadatta's plots
hook: the boulder rolled down, the elephant sent, the split in the community (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devadatta, the cousin who asked to lead the order and was refused. Your line was the wish to lead. Today, what that wish turned into.

A slope below Vulture's Peak, outside Rajagaha. The Buddha is walking in the shade of the hill. Up on the ridge, a man shoves a large rock over the edge. The Vinaya says the rock was stopped before it reached him, but a splinter broke off, struck the Buddha's foot, and drew blood. The man on the ridge is Devadatta. The Cullavagga tells his story as a chain: hired men on a road, a falling rock, an elephant set loose, and last, the one the text slows down for.
screen: `A ROCK FROM VULTURE'S PEAK.` → `A SPLINTER, AND BLOOD.` → `A CHAIN OF PLOTS.`

segments.voice: First, the hired men. In the Vinaya's telling, Devadatta sends men to kill the Buddha on a road. One by one they arrive, lose their nerve, sit down, and hear him teach. They go home as followers. Second, the rock, which Devadatta tries himself. Afterward, the Vinaya has the Buddha tell his monks that no one can take a Tathagata's life by violence. Third, the elephant. Devadatta gets the keepers to turn Nalagiri, a fierce elephant, loose on the road where the Buddha walks for alms. People scatter. The Buddha meets him with loving-kindness, metta, and the text says the elephant lowers his trunk, takes dust from the Buddha's feet, scatters it on his own head, and backs away. Fourth, the split, and here the story changes key. Devadatta goes after the community. He proposes five strict rules: live in the forest, eat only alms food, wear only rag robes, sleep under trees, eat no fish or meat. They sound devout. The Buddha answers that any monk who wishes may keep them, but he won't make them binding on all. Devadatta says this proves the Buddha has gone soft, gathers newly ordained monks, and leads them away to Gayasisa. The Buddha had already warned him that splitting the sangha is a grave thing, and tradition says it is one of the deeds that bring the heaviest results. But the chapter doesn't end with the split. Sariputta and Moggallana walk to Gayasisa, teach the young monks, and bring them home.
screen: `HIRED MEN WHO SAT DOWN TO LISTEN.` · `THE ROCK, AND THE SPLINTER.` · `NALAGIRI LOWERS HIS TRUNK.` · `FIVE RULES, AND A SPLIT.` · then, large: `THE SPLIT.`

segments.voice: Let one small split come to mind: two friends who stopped talking, a family thread gone quiet, a coworker you've been routing around. See where you stand in it, and look for one small step back across the line, a question or a plain hello. You don't have to take it yet; just find it, and hold it while the breath moves.
Devadatta's plots. Hired men, a rock, a fierce elephant, and finally a split in the sangha, the one the Buddha called grave. Today's word.
Your line: the split. A rock wounds a foot; a split wounds the thing that carries the teaching forward. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Teachers in Theravada communities tell Devadatta's plots from the Vinaya as a warning about envy and ambition, and the scene of the elephant Nalagiri calmed by loving-kindness appears in Buddhist art and in retellings of the Buddha's life.

fork.setup: Devadatta asks the Buddha to make five strict rules binding on every monk: forest, alms food only, rag robes, sleeping under trees, no fish or meat. what does the Buddha say?
options: let anyone who wishes keep them, but require none.
fork.reveal: he leaves them open to anyone who wishes and refuses to require them. Devadatta uses the refusal to split the community.

original.note: Pali saṅghabheda: a split in the sangha, the community of monks and nuns.

trapdoor: what you thought: a villain who tried to kill the Buddha.
what it means: the attacks on his body fail one by one; the plot the story weighs most is the split in the community.
what a scholar hears: the plots are told in the Cullavagga's chapter on splitting the sangha, so the whole story sits inside the rules for what counts as a schism.

chat.says: Why does the story treat Devadatta's split as worse than the rock?
options: A rock wounds a foot; a split wounds the community that carries the teaching.
Because the rock missed, so it never really counted as an attack.
Because the five rules he proposed were wrong for any monk to keep.
chat.meaning: The Buddha warned that splitting the sangha is grave: a rock wounds one foot, but a split wounds what carries the teaching forward.

Rajagaha.meaning: a city of the Buddha's time; Vulture's Peak stands outside it

Tathagata.meaning: a title the Buddha uses for himself

Nalagiri.meaning: the fierce elephant Devadatta set loose

Gayasisa.meaning: where Devadatta led the newly ordained monks

sangha.meaning: the community of the Buddha's followers

sources.ref: Vinaya, Cullavagga 7 (the hired men, the rock, Nalagiri, the five rules, the split, the return from Gayasisa)

notes: Cullavagga 7.3–7.4: confirm the order of the plots as told (hired men, then the rock from Vulture's Peak, then Nalagiri, then the five rules and the split) and the details paraphrased: the splinter drawing blood; the Buddha saying a Tathagata cannot be deprived of life by violence; the elephant taking dust from his feet and scattering it on its head.

Five rules: confirm the list as paraphrased (forest dwelling, alms only, rag robes, tree-root dwelling, no fish or meat) and that the Buddha allowed them optionally. The Vinaya adds an exception about sleeping under trees in the rainy season; omitted here.
'Later tradition counts it among the heaviest deeds': refers to the five anantariya kammas, which include causing a schism and drawing a Buddha's blood. Confirm phrasing.
Devadatta is said to have taken newly ordained Vajjian monks to Gayasisa; the number is omitted under the claims rule.
